The first revolt against the Ceaușescu regime was the miners' strike along the Jiu River in 1977, represented with the slogan "Down with the red bourgeoisie"

The strike ended with promises, but many people were arrested after the strike, sent to psychiatric hospitals and forced labor, beaten by security forces Securitate and subjected to surveillance for years after the strike.

The miners responsible were kindly sent for "treatment", with regime doctors exposing them to x-rays for five minutes. These soon became ill with cancer and died a horrific death.

The last turning point was, when the authorities decided to expel the Hungarian Protestant pastor Lázsl Tökés, followed by a demonstrations on December 18, 1989.

At the time Nicolae Ceauşescu was on a state visit to Iran, when he was informed that demonstrations were spreading across the country. So he decided to address the people immediately after his arrival from Tehran, from the famous balcony of the seat of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Romania.

This rally should be regime-based and in his support, but the opposite happened. The next day, Ceauşescu tried again, but with same opposition.

It became clear to him that only the Securitate remained loyal to him, while the rest of the state authorities denied him obedience.

Ceauşescu and his wife wanted to escape by helicopter, which, however, did not take them far, because it was allegedly dysfunctional.

They wanted to continue with a car whose engine had also failed. The next car arriving took them to the military barracks in Târgoviște, in front of the firing squad.

Thus ended the Communist dictator, who commanded the labeling of every typewriter in the country to have a total control over the people, and who was providing informations to state enemies in return for his private payment; along with his cruel, primitive and ugly wife, whose image had to hang in every science and education room. That was 30 years ago on these days.
